chapters.title: Day 1: Introduction to R and RStudio

body.text: R is a free, open-source programming language and environment used for statistical computing, data analysis, and data visualization.
R is widely used by data scientists, researchers, statisticians, and analysts to work with data, build models, and create charts and reports.

items: Statistical Analysis
Data Visualization
Data Cleaning
Machine Learning
Report Automation

body.text: R was created by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman and is maintained by the R Foundation.
RStudio is an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) for R. It provides a console, script editor, environment viewer, and plots panel in one window.

rows: Write and save R scripts (.R files)
Run R code directly, line by line
View variables and data currently in memory

body.code:
print("Hello, World!")
[1] "Hello, World!"

body.text: Comments are lines ignored by R, used to explain code. In R, a comment starts with a # symbol.

body.code:
# This is a comment
print(5 + 3)   # adds two numbers

body.text: R runs code line by line in the Console, and full programs are usually saved as .R script files.

questions.question: What type of language is R?
questions.explanation: R is a language and environment built for statistical computing and graphics.

questions.question: What is RStudio?
questions.explanation: RStudio is an Integrated Development Environment used to write and run R code.

questions.question: Which symbol is used to write a comment in R?
questions.explanation: A single # starts a comment in R.

questions.question: What does the %% operator do?
questions.explanation: %% is the modulus operator; it returns the remainder of a division.

questions.question: Which panel in RStudio is used to write and save R scripts?
questions.explanation: The Source panel is used to write and save .R script files.

tasks: Open RStudio and print your name using the print() function.
Write R code (using comments) to calculate the area of a rectangle with length 12 and width 5.
Use the console to calculate 17 %% 4 and 17 %/% 4, and note the difference.
Create a new R script file, add a comment describing what it does, and save it as day1_practice.R.

chapters.title: Day 2: Variables and Data Types

concept.title: Variables and Data Types in R

body.text: A variable is a name used to store a value in memory so it can be reused later in the program.

body.code:
x <- 10
name <- "Rahul"
print(x)
print(name)

body.text: In R, the assignment operator <- is preferred over = for assigning values to variables.

items: Must start with a letter or a dot (not followed by a number)
Can contain letters, numbers, dot (.) and underscore (_)
Case-sensitive: age and Age are different
Cannot use reserved words like TRUE, if, function

body.code:
x <- 10
class(x)          # "numeric"
y <- as.character(x)
class(y)           # "character"

x <- 25
print(x)
cat("Value of x is", x, "\n")

body.text: Use cat() when you want to combine text and variable values in one readable line.

items: Variables store data using the <- operator.
R has numeric, integer, character, logical, and complex data types.
class() checks a variable's type; as.*() functions convert between types.
print() and cat() are used to display output.

questions.question: Which operator is commonly used to assign a value to a variable in R?
questions.explanation: The <- operator is the standard way to assign values in R.

questions.question: Which of these is a valid variable name in R?
questions.explanation: student_name follows R's variable naming rules; the others are invalid or reserved.

questions.question: What will class(TRUE) return?
questions.explanation: TRUE and FALSE are logical values in R.

questions.question: Which function converts a variable to character type?
questions.explanation: as.character() converts a value into a character (text) type.

questions.question: Which function is used to display text and variable values together?
questions.explanation: cat() concatenates and prints text and variables together on one line.

tasks: Create variables for your name, age, and city, then print all three using cat().
Check the class of TRUE, 3.14, 'R', and 10L using class().
Convert the number 100 into a character and confirm using class().
Try creating a variable named 2score and observe the error R gives you.

chapters.title: Day 3: Operators in R

body.code:
5 == 5   # TRUE
5 != 3   # TRUE
5 > 10   # FALSE

age <- 20
age > 18 & age < 60   # TRUE

body.text: <- and = both assign values, but <- is the conventional style in R scripts.

body.code:
marks <- 85
result <- marks >= 40
print(result)   # TRUE

items: Arithmetic operators perform mathematical calculations.
Relational operators compare values and return TRUE/FALSE.
Logical operators combine multiple conditions.
<- is the preferred assignment operator in R.

questions.question: What does the operator == do in R?
questions.explanation: == is a relational operator that checks if two values are equal.

questions.question: What is the result of 10 %/% 3?
questions.explanation: %/% performs integer division, so 10 %/% 3 = 3.

questions.question: Which operator represents logical AND for single values?
questions.explanation: && evaluates a single logical AND comparison.

questions.question: What does the ! operator do?
questions.explanation: ! negates a logical value, turning TRUE into FALSE and vice versa.

questions.question: What will 7 != 7 return?
questions.explanation: != checks inequality; since 7 equals 7, the result is FALSE.

tasks: Write R code to check if a number stored in a variable is even using %%.
Create two variables, marks1 and marks2, and check which one is greater.
Write a logical expression to check if age is between 18 and 60 using & operator.
Predict and then verify the output of: (5 > 3) | (2 > 10)

chapters.title: Day 4: Introduction to Vectors

body.text: A vector is the most basic data structure in R. It is a sequence of elements of the same data type.

body.code:
marks <- c(80, 90, 70, 60)
names <- c("Amit", "Riya", "John")

body.text: The c() function ('combine') is used to create vectors in R.

rows: Create a sequence with a step

body.code:
nums <- 1:10
evens <- seq(2, 20, by = 2)
repeated <- rep("A", 3)

body.text: R uses 1-based indexing, meaning the first element is at position 1, not 0.

body.code:
marks <- c(80, 90, 70, 60)
marks[1]     # 80
marks[2:3]   # 90 70
marks[-1]    # all except the first element

marks <- c(80, 90, 70, 60)
length(marks)  # 4
mean(marks)    # 75
sort(marks)    # 60 70 80 90

items: A vector stores multiple values of the same type.
c(), :, seq(), and rep() are used to create vectors.
Vector indexing in R starts at 1.
length(), sum(), mean(), max(), min(), and sort() operate on vectors.

questions.question: Which function is used to create a vector in R?
questions.explanation: c() combines values into a vector.

questions.question: In R, what is the index of the first element of a vector?
questions.explanation: R uses 1-based indexing, so the first element is at index 1.

questions.question: What does 1:5 produce?
questions.explanation: The colon operator creates a sequence from 1 to 5.

questions.question: Which function returns the number of elements in a vector?
questions.explanation: length() returns how many elements a vector contains.

questions.question: What does marks[-1] do if marks <- c(80,90,70)?
options: Returns all elements except the first
questions.explanation: A negative index excludes that position, returning all other elements.

tasks: Create a vector of 5 subject marks and calculate their sum and average.
Create a vector of numbers from 1 to 50 using the seq() function with a step of 5.
Create a vector of your 3 favorite fruits and print the second one.
Create a numeric vector and print it sorted in descending order using sort(..., decreasing = TRUE).

chapters.title: Day 5: Basic Input and Output

concept.title: Basic Input and Output in R

rows: Displays a single R object with its structure
Prints text and values together, without quotes
Joins strings/values into one string, separated by a space

body.code:
name <- "Asha"
age <- 22
print(name)
cat("Name:", name, "Age:", age, "\n")
msg <- paste("Hello", name)
print(msg)

body.text: The readline() function is used to take input from the user in an interactive R console session.

body.code:
name <- readline(prompt = "Enter your name: ")
cat("Hello,", name, "\n")

body.text: readline() only works in an interactive R session (console), not when running a script non-interactively.

body.code:
age <- as.numeric(readline(prompt = "Enter your age: "))
cat("You are", age, "years old\n")

body.text: Always convert readline() input using as.numeric() before doing calculations, since it is read as text by default.

items: print() and cat() display output; cat() is used for combined text and values.
paste() and paste0() join strings together.
readline() takes user input, always returned as character text.
as.numeric() converts text input to numbers for calculations.

questions.question: Which function joins text without adding a space between values?
questions.explanation: paste0() joins values with no separator by default.

questions.question: What data type does readline() always return?
questions.explanation: readline() always returns the input as character text.

questions.question: Which function rounds 3.14159 to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: round(x, digits) rounds a number to the given number of decimal places.

questions.question: What must you do before performing math on readline() input?
questions.explanation: Since readline() returns text, it must be converted with as.numeric() before calculations.

questions.question: Which function is best for printing labeled output like 'Name: Asha'?
questions.explanation: cat() combines labels and variable values into one readable printed line.

tasks: Write a script that takes your name as input and prints 'Welcome, <name>'.
Take two numbers as input using readline() and as.numeric(), then print their sum.
Use paste() to combine your first and last name into a full name.
Round the value 7.98765 to 3 decimal places using round().

chapters.title: Day 6: Control Structures - if, else, ifelse

concept.title: Decision Making in R: if, else, ifelse

body.text: The if statement runs a block of code only when a given condition is TRUE.
ifelse() is a vectorized shortcut useful for applying a condition to every element of a vector at once.

body.code:
marks <- c(30, 55, 90, 20)
result <- ifelse(marks >= 40, "Pass", "Fail")
print(result)
# "Fail" "Pass" "Pass" "Fail"

items: if runs code only when a condition is TRUE.
else and else if handle alternate conditions.
ifelse() applies a condition across an entire vector at once.
Conditions must return TRUE or FALSE (logical values).

questions.question: What does the if statement do?
options: Runs code only when a condition is TRUE
questions.explanation: if executes a code block only when its condition evaluates to TRUE.

questions.question: Which function applies a condition across every element of a vector at once?
questions.explanation: ifelse() is vectorized and works element-by-element on a whole vector.

questions.question: In an if...else if...else chain, when is the final else executed?
options: When no earlier condition is TRUE
questions.explanation: The final else runs only if none of the preceding conditions were TRUE.

questions.question: What will ifelse(c(10,25) >= 20, 'High', 'Low') return?
questions.explanation: 10 >= 20 is FALSE ('Low') and 25 >= 20 is TRUE ('High'), giving 'Low' 'High'.

questions.question: What type of value must an if() condition evaluate to?
questions.explanation: An if condition must resolve to a single logical value, TRUE or FALSE.

tasks: Write an if...else statement to check if a number is even or odd.
Write an if...else if...else chain to assign grades A/B/C/Fail based on marks.
Use ifelse() on a vector of ages to label each as 'Minor' or 'Adult'.
Write nested if statements to check if a number is positive, negative, or zero.

chapters.title: Day 7: Vectors - Naming, Recycling and Functions

body.code:
scores <- c(80, 90, 70)
names(scores) <- c("Math", "Science", "English")
print(scores)
scores["Math"]   # 80

body.text: If two vectors of unequal length are used together, R 'recycles' (repeats) the shorter vector to match the longer one's length.
R gives a warning if the longer vector length is not an exact multiple of the shorter one.

rows: Returns index positions matching a condition

body.code:
marks <- c(45, 88, 32, 91)
which(marks > 50)   # 2 4

items: Vector elements can be named using names().
Arithmetic on vectors works element-by-element.
R recycles shorter vectors to match longer ones.
Logical indexing filters a vector using a condition.

questions.question: How do you assign names to elements of a vector?
questions.explanation: The names() function assigns or retrieves names for vector elements.

questions.question: What is the recycling rule in R?
options: Shorter vectors are repeated to match longer vector length
Vectors must always be equal length
R converts vectors to lists automatically
questions.explanation: R recycles the shorter vector's values to match the length of the longer vector.

questions.question: What does marks[marks > 50] do?
options: Returns values in marks greater than 50
questions.explanation: This uses logical indexing to return only the vector values greater than 50.

questions.question: Which function returns index positions where a condition is TRUE?
questions.explanation: which() returns the positions in a vector where the condition holds TRUE.

questions.question: Which function removes duplicate values from a vector?
questions.explanation: unique() returns only the distinct values from a vector.

tasks: Create a named vector of 4 subjects and their marks, then print the mark for one subject by name.
Create two vectors of different lengths and add them; observe the recycling warning.
Use logical indexing to extract all marks above 60 from a vector.
Use which() to find the positions of all values greater than 60 in a vector.

chapters.title: Day 8: Matrices

body.text: A matrix is a two-dimensional data structure where all elements must be of the same data type, arranged in rows and columns.

body.code:
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
print(m)

m1 <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
m2 <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, byrow = FALSE)

body.text: byrow = TRUE fills the matrix row by row; byrow = FALSE (default) fills it column by column.

body.code:
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)
m[1,2]     # element in row 1, column 2
m[1,]      # entire first row
m[,2]      # entire second column

m <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)
dim(m)     # 2 2
t(m)       # transpose

m <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)
rownames(m) <- c("R1","R2")
colnames(m) <- c("C1","C2")

items: A matrix is a 2D structure with one data type throughout.
matrix() creates matrices; byrow controls fill order.
Elements are accessed using [row, column] indexing.
dim(), t(), nrow(), and ncol() describe/manipulate matrix structure.

questions.question: What is a key requirement for all elements in a matrix?
options: They must be the same data type
questions.explanation: All elements in a matrix must share the same data type.

questions.question: What does byrow = TRUE do in matrix()?
questions.explanation: byrow = TRUE tells R to fill the matrix values row by row instead of the default column-wise order.

questions.question: How do you access the element in row 2, column 3 of matrix m?
questions.explanation: Matrix elements are accessed with square brackets as m[row, column].

questions.question: Which function returns the number of rows and columns of a matrix?
questions.explanation: dim() returns a vector with the number of rows and columns.

questions.question: Which function transposes a matrix (swaps rows and columns)?
questions.explanation: t() returns the transpose of a matrix.

tasks: Create a 3x3 matrix of numbers 1 to 9 filled row-wise, and print it.
Access and print the second row and the third column of that matrix separately.
Name the rows and columns of a 2x2 matrix and print it with names.
Create two 2x2 matrices and multiply them using the %*% operator.

chapters.title: Day 9: Lists

body.text: A list is a flexible R data structure that can hold elements of different data types together - numbers, text, vectors, even other lists.

body.code:
person <- list(name = "Riya", age = 24, marks = c(85, 90, 78))
print(person)

person$name        # "Riya"
person[["age"]]    # 24
person[[3]]        # 85 90 78

body.text: Use $ or [[ ]] to access a single element's actual value. Using single [ ] returns a sub-list, not the raw value.

body.code:
person$city <- "Delhi"      # add a new element
person$age <- 25            # update an element
person$age <- NULL           # remove an element

rows: Number of elements in the list
Converts a list to a flat vector
Displays the structure of a list

body.code:
length(person)
names(person)

student <- list(name = "Amit", scores = list(math = 90, sci = 85))
student$scores$math   # 90

items: A list can store multiple data types together, unlike a vector.
$ and [[ ]] extract actual values; [ ] returns a sub-list.
Elements can be added, updated, or removed easily.
Lists can be nested inside other lists.

questions.question: What makes a list different from a vector?
options: A list can hold multiple data types together
A list can only hold numbers
questions.explanation: Unlike a vector, a list can store elements of different data types together.

questions.question: Which symbol is commonly used to access a named list element?
questions.explanation: The $ symbol accesses a named element of a list directly.

questions.question: What does single bracket [ ] return when used on a list?
questions.explanation: Single brackets [ ] return a smaller list, while [[ ]] returns the actual value.

questions.question: Which function converts a list into a flat vector?
questions.explanation: unlist() flattens a list's elements into a single vector.

questions.question: How do you remove an element from a list named 'age'?
questions.explanation: Assigning NULL to a list element removes it from the list.

tasks: Create a list to store a student's name, roll number, and a vector of 3 subject marks.
Access the student's name using $ and their second mark using [[ ]].
Add a new element 'city' to the list, then update it, then remove it.
Create a nested list representing a person with an address list inside it (city, pincode).

chapters.title: Day 10: Data Frames - Introduction

body.text: A data frame is a table-like structure in R, similar to a spreadsheet or a database table. Each column can hold a different data type, but all columns must have the same length.

body.code:
students <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Amit", "Riya", "John"),
  Age = c(21, 22, 20),
  Marks = c(85, 90, 75)
)
print(students)

rows: Shows structure of the data frame

body.code:
str(students)
head(students, 2)
ncol(students)

body.text: 3. Accessing Data Frame Columns and Rows

body.code:
students$Name          # entire Name column
students[1, ]          # entire first row
students[, 2]          # entire second column
students[1, "Marks"]   # single cell

students$Grade <- c("B", "A", "C")
print(students)
students[students$Marks > 80, ]

items: A data frame is a table with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.
data.frame() creates one from equal-length vectors.
$ accesses columns; [row, col] accesses specific rows/cells.
New columns can be added directly, and rows filtered using conditions.

questions.question: A data frame is most similar to which structure?
questions.explanation: A data frame organizes data into rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.

questions.question: What must be true about all columns in a data frame?
options: They must be the same length
They must have the same name
questions.explanation: All columns in a data frame must have the same number of elements (rows).

questions.question: Which function displays the structure of a data frame?
questions.explanation: str() shows the structure, including column types, of a data frame.

questions.question: How do you access the 'Marks' column of a data frame named students?
questions.explanation: The $ operator accesses a named column in a data frame.

questions.question: How would you filter students with Marks greater than 80?
questions.explanation: Row filtering uses students[condition, ] to keep only matching rows.

tasks: Create a data frame of 4 students with Name, Age, and Marks columns.
Use str() and head() to explore the data frame you created.
Add a new column 'Result' that says 'Pass' or 'Fail' based on Marks (you can assign manually for now).
Filter and print only the students whose Age is greater than 20.

chapters.title: Day 11: Factors

body.text: A factor is used in R to store categorical data - data with a fixed, limited set of possible values, such as gender, blood group, or grade.

body.code:
grade <- factor(c("A", "B", "A", "C", "B"))
print(grade)
levels(grade)   # "A" "B" "C"

items: Save memory by storing categories as integer codes internally
Useful for statistical modeling and grouping
Ensure only valid categories are allowed

body.text: Factors can represent an inherent order, such as low/medium/high, using the ordered argument.

body.code:
level <- factor(c("Low","High","Medium"),
   levels = c("Low","Medium","High"),
   ordered = TRUE)
level
level[1] < level[2]   # TRUE

rows: Converts factor to its underlying integer codes

body.code:
grade <- factor(c("A","B","A","C","B"))
table(grade)

items: Factors store categorical data with a fixed set of levels.
levels() lists the distinct categories in a factor.
Ordered factors capture ranking, such as Low < Medium < High.
table() is useful to count how many times each category appears.

questions.question: What kind of data is a factor best suited for?
questions.explanation: Factors are designed to represent categorical data with fixed categories.

questions.question: Which function lists the distinct categories of a factor?
questions.explanation: levels() returns the unique category values of a factor.

questions.question: What does ordered = TRUE in factor() indicate?
options: The categories have a ranked order
questions.explanation: ordered = TRUE tells R the factor levels have a meaningful ranking, e.g. Low < Medium < High.

questions.question: Which function counts how many times each category appears in a factor?
questions.explanation: table() tabulates the frequency of each level in a factor.

questions.question: Which function returns the number of distinct levels in a factor?
questions.explanation: nlevels() returns the count of unique category levels in a factor.

tasks: Create a factor for 6 students' grades (A, B, C) and print its levels.
Use table() to count how many students got each grade.
Create an ordered factor for shirt sizes: Small, Medium, Large and compare two sizes.
Convert a grade factor to its underlying integer codes using as.integer().

chapters.title: Day 12: Arrays

body.text: An array is a data structure that can store data in more than two dimensions. While a matrix is 2D, an array can be 3D or higher.

body.code:
arr <- array(1:24, dim = c(2,3,4))
print(dim(arr))   # 2 3 4

arr <- array(1:12, dim = c(2,3,2))
print(arr)

body.text: An array is essentially a vector reshaped into multiple dimensions; all elements must be the same data type.

body.code:
arr <- array(1:12, dim = c(2,3,2))
arr[1,2,1]     # single element
arr[,,1]       # entire first 'layer' (matrix)

items: An array extends a matrix to 3 or more dimensions.
array() reshapes a vector of values using the dim argument.
Elements are accessed with array[row, col, layer] indexing.
All array elements must share the same data type.

questions.question: How many dimensions can an array have, compared to a matrix?
questions.explanation: Unlike a matrix (strictly 2D), an array can have 2 or more dimensions.

questions.question: Which argument in array() defines its shape?
questions.explanation: The dim argument specifies the dimensions of the array, e.g. dim = c(2,3,4).

questions.question: What must be true of all elements inside an array?
options: They must be the same data type
questions.explanation: Like vectors and matrices, arrays require all elements to share one data type.

questions.question: How do you access the entire first 'layer' of a 3D array named arr?
questions.explanation: arr[,,1] selects all rows and columns from the first layer (third dimension index 1).

questions.question: Which structure allows different data types in different columns?
questions.explanation: A data frame allows each column to have its own data type, unlike vectors, matrices, and arrays.

tasks: Create a 3D array of dimensions 2x2x3 filled with numbers 1 to 12.
Print the second 'layer' of that array.
Access a single specific element from the array using 3 indices.
In your own words (as a comment in your script), write the difference between a matrix and an array.

chapters.title: Day 13: Loops - for

body.text: A loop is used to repeat a block of code multiple times, which saves time and avoids repetitive code.
This loop runs once for every value in the sequence 1:5, assigning each value to i in turn.
4. Loop With a Counter and Sum
Prefer vectorized functions (like sum() or sapply()) over loops in R when possible - loops can be slower on large data.

items: for loops repeat code for each value in a sequence or vector.
The loop variable takes each value from the sequence in turn.
Loops can be nested to handle multi-level repetition.
R also supports vectorized alternatives that often run faster than loops.

questions.question: What does a for loop do?
options: Repeats code for each value in a sequence
questions.explanation: A for loop executes a block of code once for every value in a given sequence.

questions.question: What will `for (i in 1:3) print(i)` output?
questions.explanation: The loop prints 1, then 2, then 3, once for each value in the sequence 1:3.

questions.question: Can a for loop iterate directly over a character vector?
questions.explanation: A for loop can iterate over any vector, including character vectors.

questions.question: What is a nested loop?
options: A loop placed inside another loop
questions.explanation: A nested loop is a loop written inside the body of another loop.

questions.question: Which is generally recommended for large-scale operations in R?
options: Avoid loops entirely, even for small tasks
questions.explanation: R favors vectorized operations/functions over loops for better performance on large data.

tasks: Write a for loop to print numbers from 1 to 20.
Write a for loop to calculate the sum of the first 15 natural numbers.
Write a for loop that prints each name from a vector of 5 friends' names.
Write a nested for loop to print a simple 5x5 multiplication table.

chapters.title: Day 14: Loops - while, repeat, break and next

body.text: A while loop repeats code as long as a given condition remains TRUE.
Always make sure the loop variable changes inside the loop, or the while loop will run forever (infinite loop).
A repeat loop runs indefinitely until a break statement stops it explicitly.
break immediately exits the loop it is inside, regardless of the loop condition.
next skips the current iteration and moves on to the next one, without exiting the loop.

items: while repeats code as long as a condition stays TRUE.
repeat runs forever until a break is reached.
break exits a loop entirely; next skips to the following iteration.
Loop variables must be updated to avoid infinite loops.

questions.question: When does a while loop stop repeating?
questions.explanation: A while loop continues as long as its condition is TRUE and stops once it becomes FALSE.

questions.question: How does a repeat loop stop?
questions.explanation: A repeat loop has no built-in condition and must be stopped with break.

questions.question: What does the break statement do?
questions.explanation: break immediately terminates the loop it is placed in.

questions.question: What does the next statement do?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration and continues to the next
questions.explanation: next skips remaining code in the current iteration and proceeds to the next one.

questions.question: What commonly causes an infinite while loop?
options: Forgetting to update the loop variable
questions.explanation: If the loop variable never changes to make the condition FALSE, the while loop runs forever.

tasks: Write a while loop to print numbers from 10 down to 1.
Write a repeat loop that prints numbers 1 to 5 and stops using break.
Write a for loop from 1 to 10 that skips number 7 using next.
Write a while loop that keeps doubling a number starting from 1, stopping once it exceeds 100.

chapters.title: Day 15: Functions - Basics and Arguments

body.text: A function is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task. R has many built-in functions, and users can also create their own custom functions.
A function argument can have a default value, used automatically if the caller doesn't supply one.

items: Functions are created using the function() keyword.
Arguments allow functions to accept input values.
Default values are used automatically when an argument is omitted.
Arguments can be passed by position or by name.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to define a function in R?
questions.explanation: R uses the function() keyword to define a function.

questions.question: What is an argument in a function?
options: An input value the function accepts
questions.explanation: Arguments are the input values a function accepts to perform its task.

questions.question: What happens if an argument has a default value and is not supplied?
options: The default value is used automatically
questions.explanation: If an argument isn't given by the caller, its default value defined in the function is used instead.

questions.question: In info(age = 25, name = 'Sam'), what technique is being used?
questions.explanation: This calls the function using named arguments, so order doesn't matter.

questions.question: Can a function in R be defined without any arguments?
options: No, it always needs at least one

chapters.title: Day 16: Functions - Return Values and Scope

body.text: A function can send a value back to the caller using return(), or simply by evaluating it as the last line of the function.

body.code:
square <- function(x) x^2
result <- square(5)
print(result)   # 25

body.text: A variable created inside a function is 'local' - it exists only inside that function and disappears once the function finishes running.

body.code:
x <- 10   # global variable
myFunc <- function() {
  x <- 5   # local variable, separate from global x
  print(x) # 5
}
myFunc()
print(x)   # 10 (unchanged)

body.text: Functions can read global variables, but changes made to a local variable of the same name do not affect the global one.
4. Multiple Return Values Using a List

items: return() (or the last line) sends a value back from a function.
Function outputs can be stored in variables for reuse.
Variables created inside a function are local to that function.
A list can be used to return multiple values from one function.

questions.question: How can a function return a value in R?
options: Using return() or as the last evaluated line
Using return() only, nothing else works
questions.explanation: A function returns a value either explicitly with return() or implicitly via its last evaluated expression.

options: A variable available everywhere in the program
A variable that exists only inside the function where it's created
questions.explanation: Local variables are created and only accessible within the function they are defined in.

questions.question: If x <- 10 globally, and a function sets a local x <- 5 and returns, what is the global x afterward?
questions.explanation: The local x inside the function is separate; the global x remains unchanged at 10.

questions.question: How can a function return multiple values at once?
questions.explanation: Returning a list lets a function bundle and return multiple values together.

questions.explanation: Local variables exist only during the function call and are discarded once it completes.

chapters.title: Day 17: The apply Family - sapply and lapply

body.text: The apply family of functions lets you apply a function to every element of a vector, list, or data structure without writing an explicit loop - this is a very common R style.
lapply() applies a function to each element of a list or vector, and always returns a list.

body.code:
nums <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
result <- lapply(nums, function(x) x^2)
print(result)   # a list: 1, 4, 9, 16

body.text: sapply() works like lapply(), but tries to simplify the result into a vector or matrix instead of a list.

body.code:
nums <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
result <- sapply(nums, function(x) x^2)
print(result)   # 1 4 9 16 (a vector)

rows: Returns a simplified vector/matrix when possible

body.code:
words <- c("apple", "banana", "kiwi")
sapply(words, nchar)   # 5 6 4, named by input value

body.text: Use sapply() when you want a clean vector result; use lapply() when you specifically need a list, e.g., for mixed-type outputs.

items: The apply family replaces many explicit loops in R.
lapply() always returns a list.
sapply() simplifies output into a vector or matrix when possible.
Both can be used with built-in or custom (anonymous) functions.

chapters.title: Day 18: The apply Family - apply, mapply and vapply

body.text: 1. apply() - For Matrices and Data Frames
apply() applies a function across the rows or columns of a matrix or data frame, controlled by the MARGIN argument.

body.code:
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)
apply(m, 1, sum)   # sum of each row
apply(m, 2, sum)   # sum of each column

body.text: mapply() applies a function to corresponding elements of two or more vectors simultaneously.
vapply() is like sapply(), but requires you to specify the expected type of output in advance, making it safer and slightly faster.

body.code:
vapply(c(1,2,3), function(x) x^2, FUN.VALUE = numeric(1))
# 1 4 9

rows: Rows/columns of a matrix or data frame
Any list/vector, output as a list
Same as sapply(), with guaranteed output type

items: apply() works across rows (MARGIN=1) or columns (MARGIN=2) of matrices/data frames.
mapply() applies a function over multiple vectors in parallel.
vapply() is a safer, type-checked version of sapply().
Choosing the right apply function depends on the input structure and desired output.

body.text: sprintf() builds formatted strings using placeholders, similar to printf in other languages.

name <- "Riya"

chapters.title: Day 20: Regular Expressions - grepl, gsub, grep

body.text: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern used to search, match, or manipulate text based on rules, not just exact text.
grepl() returns TRUE or FALSE depending on whether a pattern is found in a string.

body.code:
grepl("an", "banana")     # TRUE
grepl("^b", "banana")     # TRUE (starts with b)
grepl("a$", "banana")     # TRUE (ends with a)

body.text: grep() returns the index positions (or the values) of elements in a vector that match a pattern.

body.code:
words <- c("apple", "banana", "grape")
grep("an", words)              # 2
grep("an", words, value = TRUE) # "banana"

gsub("[0-9]", "", "Room A101")     # "Room A" (removes digits)
gsub("\\s+", " ", "R   is   fun")   # collapses multiple spaces into one

items: Regular expressions describe text patterns for searching and matching.
grepl() checks TRUE/FALSE for a pattern match.
grep() returns positions or matching values.
gsub() replaces text that matches a pattern, useful for cleaning data.

questions.question: What does grepl() return?

questions.question: What does the ^ symbol mean in a regex pattern?

questions.question: What does grep('an', words, value = TRUE) return?
questions.explanation: value = TRUE tells grep() to return the matching strings themselves, not their positions.

questions.question: Which function is best suited for removing all digits from a string?
questions.explanation: gsub() can replace all digit characters (matched using a pattern like [0-9]) with an empty string.

questions.question: What does [0-9] represent in a regex pattern?
questions.explanation: [0-9] matches any single digit character from 0 to 9.

body.text: After cleaning or analyzing data in R, you often need to save results back to a file for sharing or reuse, such as a CSV file.

chapters.title: Day 24: Data Cleaning - Missing Values and Subsetting

body.text: NA represents a missing or unavailable value in R. Almost any calculation involving NA also results in NA, unless handled explicitly.

body.code:
marks <- c(80, NA, 90, NA, 70)
sum(marks)          # NA
sum(marks, na.rm = TRUE)   # 240 (ignores NA values)

is.na(marks)          # FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE
sum(is.na(marks))     # 2 (count of NAs)

clean <- marks[!is.na(marks)]
print(clean)   # 80 90 70

body.text: 4. Removing Rows With NA From a Data Frame

body.code: clean_df <- na.omit(students)

students[students$Marks > 75, ]                 # rows where Marks > 75
students[, c("Name", "Marks")]                   # only specific columns
subset(students, Marks > 75, select = c(Name, Marks))

body.text: The subset() function is a convenient shortcut for filtering rows and selecting columns together.

is.na() detects missing values; na.rm = TRUE ignores them in functions like sum().
na.omit() removes rows containing any NA from a data frame.

chapters.title: Day 25: dplyr Basics - filter, select, mutate

body.text: dplyr is a popular R package that provides simple, readable functions for manipulating data frames. It must be installed and loaded before use.

install.packages("dplyr")   # run once

  filter(Marks > 70) %>%

chapters.title: Day 28: Introduction to ggplot2

body.text: ggplot2 is a powerful and popular R package for creating polished, layered data visualizations, based on the 'Grammar of Graphics'.

body.code:
install.packages("ggplot2")   # run once
library(ggplot2)                # run every session

body.text: A ggplot2 chart is built in layers: start with ggplot(), specify data and aesthetics (aes), then add a geometry layer with a + sign.

body.code:
ggplot(students, aes(x = Name, y = Marks)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue")

ggplot(students, aes(x = Name, y = Marks)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "darkgreen") +
  labs(title = "Student Marks", x = "Student", y = "Marks")

ggplot(students, aes(x = Age, y = Marks)) +
  geom_point(color = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Age vs Marks")

items: ggplot2 builds charts in layers using the + operator.
aes() maps data columns to visual properties like x and y axes.
geom_*() functions define the chart type: bar, point, line, histogram, etc.
labs() adds titles and axis labels to make charts easy to read.

questions.question: What must be loaded before using ggplot2 functions?

questions.question: In ggplot2, what does aes() do?

chapters.title: Day 30: Mini Project - Student Performance Analysis

concept.title: Final Mini Project: Bringing It All Together

body.text: In this final project, you will use everything learned over the past 29 days - vectors, data frames, functions, loops, dplyr, and visualization - to analyze a small student performance dataset.

body.code:
students <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Amit","Riya","John","Sara","Vikram"),
  Age = c(21, 22, 20, 23, 21),
  Math = c(78, 92, 55, 88, 40),
  Science = c(82, 89, 60, 95, 45)
)

body.text: Use mutate() (or base R) to calculate each student's total and average marks, then assign a Result.

body.code:
students$Total <- students$Math + students$Science
students$Average <- students$Total / 2
students$Result <- ifelse(students$Average >= 40, "Pass", "Fail")

summary(students$Average)
mean(students$Average)
table(students$Result)

barplot(students$Average, names.arg = students$Name,
        main = "Average Marks per Student", col = "steelblue")

body.text: 7. Step 6: Filter and Sort With dplyr

body.code:
library(dplyr)
students %>%
  filter(Result == "Pass") %>%
  arrange(desc(Average))
